label: Precautionary Environmentalism / Degrowth
summary: A family of views holding that Earth's biosphere has intrinsic value and finite limits that industrial growth is overshooting. Deep ecology rejects anthropocentrism; degrowth economics advocates planned contraction of material throughput in rich countries; the precautionary principle shifts the burden of proof onto new technologies.
variants: Deep ecology (spiritual-ecocentric) vs degrowth (political-economic, often eco-socialist) vs mainstream sustainability (reformist, growth-compatible) vs ecomodernism (which defects to the proactionary side). The bright-green/dark-green split is fundamental; social ecology (Bookchin) attacks deep ecology as misanthropic.

positions.summary: Mixed: systems science and planetary-boundaries research plus appeals to intuition, indigenous knowledge, and ecological experience; skeptical of reductionist knowledge claims.
Limits are the organizing idea: overshoot models and planetary boundaries imply knowledge cannot indefinitely outrun biophysical constraints.
Ecological science plus ethical intuition and traditional ecological wisdom; distrust of corporate and technocratic authority.
Realist about ecological limits and biophysical facts, while critical of technocratic framings of what counts as knowledge.
Growth-driven 'progress' is overshoot heading toward collapse; hope attaches only to a transformed, sufficiency-based society.
Maximal precaution — the defining position: irreversible ecological harms justify restraint even without scientific certainty; opposes geoengineering, often nuclear and GMOs.
Structural: growth imperatives of capitalism and industrialism drive outcomes; change requires systemic transformation, not individual choices.
Ecocentric anti-anthropocentrism: all living systems have value independent of usefulness to humans; humanity should reduce its impact and footprint.
Objective intrinsic value in nature (biocentric egalitarianism) and strong intergenerational duties — a realism that decenters humans.
Naturalist but holistic and ecocentric; some strands (Self-realization, Gaia-inflected ecology) shade toward the spiritual or pantheist.
Seeks systemic transformation of the economy while conserving natural systems and opposing the innovation treadmill — conservation-oriented about nature, radical about institutions.
Harmony within limits — the other defining position: humans must fit within the biosphere's boundaries; the wild has intrinsic normative authority.
Meaning found in harmonious, sufficient relation with the living Earth — 'richer in ends, simpler in means'.
Collectivist and systemic: community, commons, and civilizational-scale coordination over individual consumer choice.
